items.title: Emmanuel Sayles Interview, 1959-01-17
items.q: by me being a kid, I didn't really get a chance to go out there then

ctx.x: Well, let's go back before your time, back as far as we can, I guess. You say your father played?

Yeah, my father was one of the original men of what they call the Silver Leaf Band. It was a string band. And from what he told me, there was a man that played violin. See the name of the iPhone's? They were out in the riverfront. He played violin and sax. Do you remember him? No, I don't get it. And then he and my daddy and there was, my daddy played guitar and he on violin. And then they had a bass. And I don't remember what a bass player, but at that time, my daddy tell me they used to, all the fellas used to…
Does that look familiar, Donaldsonville Railroad Avenue?

items.title: Emmanuel Sayles Interview, 1959-01-17
items.q: he was a very close friend to the family of my mother and him. He knew my mother's sisters and brothers and all of them and my grandfather and all of them... we didn't live but two half a block from the Claiborne on the same street.

ctx.x: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . And Claiborne, I would say, was like when I came to New Orleans, like Dave Poikin was. He taught both white and colored. Because I remember there was a white student and he had to go to their house and teach them, you see. And he was very known, I mean, as a very good teacher because there were many good musicians that came in colored and white that came to be a good musician that he had actually started. Now he was…
What about the funerals out there? Are they similar to the funerals here with brass bands?
